#924. Liverpool incorrectly denied pen vs Arsenal says independent panel

Alexander Isak was not awarded a penalty during Arsenal's win at Liverpool in November despite Jurrien Timber pulling his shirt; referee Andy Madley gave nothing on-field and VAR Stuart Attwell did not intervene; independent Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel gives verdict

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty when Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak's shirt in Arsenal's victory at Anfield, an independent panel has ruled.

The Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel assesses refereeing incidents across every Premier League match and voted 4:1 that referee Andy Madley should have awarded Liverpool a spot kick.

The panel also voted 3:2 that VAR Stuart Attwell should have intervened and sent Madley to the pitchside monitor on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error.

Arsenal led 1-0 through Kai Havertz's goal, which proved to be the winner, when Isak attempted to head Bradley Barcola's cross in the 21st minute on November 1, but was pulled back by defender Timber.

One KMI panellist believed "the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress", while two panellists argued, "the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention".

Isak stayed on his feet during the incident and Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola said afterwards he would tell the striker to go down next time.

So far this season 196 KMIs have been examined, with the correct on-field decision taken in 86 per cent of cases. That rises to 97 per cent following VAR intervention.

The Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel provides an independent assessment of key decisions in every Premier League match. It is an independent group of five members: three former players or coaches, one representative from the Premier League, and one from Pro Ref, the organisation responsible for refereeing in England.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jamie Carragher: "One of the best goalscorers in the league is pulled back seven yards out and it stops him heading the ball - why does he need to make a meal of it? VAR, do your job."

Ian Wright: "He shouldn't have to make more of it. We can see it... Unless I'm pulled back, I'm going to head it as much as I can. When he pulled him, it was just about enough as he would need to go down.

"VAR is wrong in this instance. If they gave that penalty, I wouldn't sit here and say 'I can't believe they gave that'."

Gary Neville: "It's actually unnatural not to make more of it. When you get pulled and you're just about to score, you ordinarily complain like crazy. It's a very odd reaction from Isak."

Daniel Sturridge: "Unfortunately, he (Isak) has not fallen over. You're supposed to fall over, put your arms in the air and show the referee you're mad about it... to me, his reaction is almost like 'VAR, do your job'.

"But they've not done their job. He shouldn't have to make more of it - clearly, he shouldn't. Everyone can see that his arm is stretched, he [Timber] is holding him with a stretched-out arm."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher: "It depends which angle you watch it from. The first angle, you see nothing. That is the referee's angle.

"The second angle, which is what VAR looks at, and it is a lot more damning.

"VAR looks at it in slow motion, which is another thing against him. In normal speed, he grabs and grabs him quickly but let's go. Does he do enough [for a penalty]?

"What is Timber's intention? He is on the wrong side of him. Does he do enough to stop him? He [Isak] will say yes, as he is close to the ball.

"VAR would be accused of re-refereeing if it is a penalty. It is a case of damned if they do and damned if they don't.

"It has to be the case of on-field. The more I watch it, the more I think he [Timber] has taken a big chance and has got lucky."

What happens if Isak goes down? "Once a player hits the ground, there are more questions to ask.

"There is asking what has knocked him down. Has he gone down by his own momentum, has he slipped or has he been pulled or pushed?

"Once you factor that in, obviously you have a different decision. He [referee] has to deal with the situation he has seen. He has seen a little pull of the jersey and thought no penalty."

Jay Bothroyd: "Where was the referee? Every angle, I can see it is a penalty.

"He has pulled his shirt. How can none of them [referee and VAR] see that and say it is a penalty? I can't comprehend that. I don't get it.

"That is one of the most obvious penalties [I have seen]. He is running forward! He has stifled his momentum going forward, to stop him heading the ball.

"Every angle I look at, even normal time, I said it could be a penalty. I look at it now, the more I see it, the more I ask myself how they have missed it! How do they lose focus and not get that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Andoni Iraola: "The Isak one is a clear penalty. We can all see that he holds the t-shirt. The ball just goes one centimetre in front of Alex. Alex is going to hit the ball in front of the goal."

On whether the player needed to go down: "The fact that you are even asking me that shows he should have gone to the floor. If he does, they call the penalty 100 per cent.

Asked whether he will tell Alex to go down next time: "Yes, definitely."

Virgil van Dijk: "I've seen it back and I've seen it given as well on other occasions. Today it wasn't meant to be.

"The VAR doesn't notice it? There are 50 cameras. Even more. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras? It is spotted because everyone's seen it.

"In the end, it wasn't given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal."

From Arsenal's perspective, Mikel Arteta said he had not watched the incident back and had no comment when asked by Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Towards the end of the second half, Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister went down holding his face after his forehead touched with Noni Madueke's.

VAR reviewed the incident, and the Arsenal winger was not sent off. Instead, Mac Allister was booked.

The KMI panel unanimously felt the referee was correct not to show Madueke a red card as the contact was "negligible" and Mac Allister's reaction "clearly exaggerated".

The KMI panel also ruled that Ipswich Town should have been awarded a penalty in their 2-2 draw with Hull City on October 3.

Nobel Mendy was judged to have committed a holding offence against Dara O'Shea during a corner in the 18th minute, with the score still goalless.

The panel voted 4-1 that referee Tom Kirk should have awarded a penalty, while VAR Neil Davies should also have recommended an on-field review.

The majority agreed there was "a clear sustained holding offence", although one panellist felt O'Shea and Florentino Luis's actions during the incident should have been considered, meaning a penalty was not warranted.

#923. England's Bethell out of Australia tour and a doubt for South Africa Tests

Jacob Bethell has not played since July due to knee injury, will head back to the UK at the weekend after suffering a setback in training; left-hander could be fighting a battle to be fit for three-Test assignment in South Africa from December 17, live on Sky Sports

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of England's entire white-ball tour of Australia after suffering a setback on his return from injury and could now be a doubt for the Tests in South Africa.

Batter and spin bowler Bethell has not played since scoring 91 in the final one-day international against India at Lord's in July after sustaining a right knee problem that required surgery.

The 23-year-old was hoping to return for the three ODIs against Australia, which start in Perth on Friday, and the five T20 internationals that follow, but will now head back to England after a recurrence of the injury in training and is poised to see a specialist.

On Monday, Bethell was included in England's Test squad for the three-match tour of South Africa from December 17.

Fast bowler Josh Tongue had already been already ruled out of the Australia fixtures due to a toe injury.

England have called up uncapped Hampshire seamer Eddie Jack and Sussex all-rounder James Coles into the ODI squad as replacements.

Jack and Coles were already part of the T20 party.

In Bethell's absence from the ODI side, Tom Banton has formed a successful opening partnership with Ben Duckett, so his return to the XI straightaway in that format was perhaps unlikely.

If the left-hander also misses the red-ball assignments in South Africa - live in full on Sky Sports, with the opening game at Wanderers in Johannesburg - then it will ease a selection dilemma for England.

Jordan Cox struck three half-centuries in as many matches after deputising for Bethell at No 3 in the 3-0 Test rout of Pakistan.

Should Bethell be fit to face the Proteas, there may only be space for three of him, Cox, Emilio Gay and Dan Lawrence in the XI.

Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton on Jacob Bethell:

"I think it is a precautionary thing given how busy the winter is but the concern is how little cricket Bethell's had and therefore how easy is it for him to slip back into the team?

"Perhaps this makes it a bit more difficult but our best wishes to him. Let's hope it is not a significant setback.

"There is a bit of Lions cricket just ahead of the main tour of South Africa. That's the good thing for him.

"There's a camp in Pietermaritzburg and four-day Test against South Africa A so there's an opportunity there once he's fit.

"If he is fit and has had game time, then I think Bethell should bat at No 3 in the Test series. If he runs out of time, he will just have to sit on the sidelines."

ODIs 3.30am UK time, with T20s 8.15am UK time

#922. Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free)

This was the window of the midfielder for Manchester United, with three recruited: Youri Tielemans (a No 8), Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba (No 6s). Yet missing was a left-back despite the targeting of Lewis Hall, and others, plus reinforcements for the rest of a creaking rearguard. The reason? A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. Will the specialist Luke Shaw, plus the stand-in options of Parick Dorgu (a wing-back/left forward), Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui (right-backs), Lizandro Martínez (centre-back) and Baleba prove adequate? JJ

Key ins: Carlos Baleba (Brighton, £70m), Andrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m)

Key outs: Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m), Casemiro (Inter Miami, free)

Newcastle describe their transfer window as “transformative” and, with reinvention the name of the game on Tyneside, it is easy to see why. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. The deadline day arrival of the exciting 21-year-old Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille is regarded as quite a coup. Have Newcastle choreographed a triumph from a window that, at one point, looked potentially disastrous? LT

Key ins: Nico González (Manchester City, £52m), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (Lille, £51m), Bazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £30m), Amar Dedic (Benfica, £29.5m), Lukas Hornicek (Braga, £25.7m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m)

Key outs: Sandro Tonali (Tottenham, £92.5m), Bruno Guimarães (Arsenal, £75m), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona, £69.3m), Nick Woltemade (Juventus, loan), Kieran Trippier (Wolves, free)

Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Whether not sourcing a direct replacement for Anderson will hurt them remains to be seen but at least they did not panic, making it a measured window where they were able to trim the squad. Will Unwin

Key ins: Liam Delap (Chelsea, £45m), Ousmane Diomande (Sporting, £34.2m), Daniel Muñoz (Crystal Palace, £22m), Steven Benda (Fulham, free), Xaver Schlager (RB Leipzig, free)

Key outs: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City, £116m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry City, £9m), Omari Hutchinson (Milan, loan), Stefan Ortega (Olympiakos, free), Jota Silva (Olympiakos, loan), Morato (West Ham, loan)

After last summer’s 14 new faces this had been a bit of a conservative, almost slightly underwhelming, window. Or at least it was until Crystal Palace tried to hijack Sunderland’s agreement to sign the Lyon winger Malick Fofana and the two Premier League clubs engaged in an astonishing deadline day tug of war involving private jets from both sitting on the tarmac at Lyon airport and Fofana undergoing a medical in France unsure as to his destination until finally choosing Wearside. Arguably Sunderland’s biggest achievement was keeping last season’s star players. If persuading Granit Xhaka to stay rather than defect to Chelsea was vital, Régis Le Bris will be similarly delighted to have retained widely admired individuals of the calibre of Enzo Le Fée, Robin Roefs and Noah Sadiki. LT

Key ins: Malick Fofana (Lyon, £31m), Dayann Méthalie (Toulouse, £24m), Kevin Danso (Tottenham, loan), Thomas Meunier (Lille, free)

Key outs: Eliezer Mayenda (Rennes, £17.1m)

A comprehensive reboot, from back to front, featuring a club record outlay for a window and one of the most lavish by any club ever. In the first summer window since the departure of the longstanding chair Daniel Levy, the hierarchy have backed Roberto De Zerbi in an attempt to put the trauma of last season behind them. All the new signings have Premier League experience and – apart from Mateus Fernandes and Sávio – are aged 25 or over. In other words, they ought to be ready to hit the ground running. The opening two matches did not go to plan. It will get better. Won’t it? David Hytner

Key ins: Sandro Tonali (Newcastle, £92.5m), Mateus Fernandes (West Ham, £85m), Sávio (Manchester City, £75m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Brighton, £52m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Chelsea, £7m), Omar Marmoush (Manchester City, loan), Martin Dubravka (Burnley, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Chelsea, loan), Marcos Senesi (Bournemouth, free), Andy Robertson (Liverpool, free)

#921. California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare it a success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for about half of the funding to be given directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University in Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, which are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, including the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure that such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03635-6

#920. Managerial 'inconsistency' hurting Ghana - Hughton

Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right)

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

*Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards

#918. Oldham boss Mellon charged by FA following red card

Micky Mellon's Oldham Athletic side are 18th in League Two

Oldham Athletic manager Micky Mellon has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association following his red card during his side's FA Cup win over Sheffield Wednesday.

He was sent off in the 83rd minute of Sunday's tie by referee Martin Woods for appearing to move his head towards Wednesday forward Callum Slattery in an aggressive manner.

Mellon has been charged with acting in an improper manner and/or using violent conduct and he has until Friday, 13 November to respond.

Without him on the sidelines, the Latics secured an extra-time victory over the League One side to set up a second-round trip to Grimsby Town.

#916. Love Island’s Trinity Reveals Living Situation With Bryce in L.A.

Trinity Tatum exclusively told E! News at the 2026 EBONY Power 100 what her and Bryce Alakai’s life together in L.A. looks like after their Love Island USA win: “I make him come over all the time.”

Trinity Tatum and Bryce Alakai’s romance was never meant to stay in Fiji.

In fact, Tatum recently moved from her native Virginia to Los Angeles, where Alakai is based, following their win on Love Island USA season eight—and their new chapter is going swimmingly.

“I just got my apartment,” she exclusively told E! News in a joint interview with fellow islander Aniya Harvey at the 2026 EBONY Power 100 event on Nov. 9. “But it’s so funny because I literally just spent the night over Bryce’s house last night, so it’s like do a combination of I go over his house, he comes over mine.”

For them, having that balance in their relationship is crucial.

“He’s like, ‘I’m paying rent. I still have to go home,’” the 23-year-old quipped. “I make him come over all the time and he’s like, ‘Girl, I’m still paying rent to be here. L.A. rent is not cheap, honey.’”

That’s why Tatum and Alakai, 30, have “been mixing and dabbling” to get a "mix of both.” And the life they’ve built is exactly her type on paper.

“I’ve been in L.A. a lot,” she continued. “I’ve been around my man. I’ve been around all his friends and all of my girls.”

As for their holiday plans, the two will be making a splash with their loved ones.

“I am spending the holidays in Boston,” Tatum shared. “I want to spend a lot of it with my mom. We’re both spending it with both of our families.”

And Harvey is keen to do the same. After all, she revealed her plans to throw a huge holiday party in her native Atlanta, sharing she’ll be inviting “every single person.”

And that of course includes the rest of the core four ladies, including Kayda Bosse and Melanie Moreno, who Tatum shared she still talks to daily.

And Harvey, 24, makes it a point to stay connected as well. As she put it, “I feel like we do a good job of being in tune with one another.”

But in addition to finding both love and friendship in the Villa, the core four have also found success, a fact that Tatum shared they still “process” every day.

“I feel like every time we go to an event like this or anything we’ve been invited to, we are processing it,” she said. “Like, wow we’re really here.”

And Harvey echoed that sentiment, adding, “We take it in every single day. It’s such a blessing.”

Keep reading for a closer look at where more Love Island couples stand today…

Nathan Massey & Cara De La Hoyde: Married

The ultimate Love Island success story, Nathan and Cara were declared season two's winning pair after meeting in the villa in 2016.

Once Cara learned she was pregnant with their first child in May 2017, the couple briefly split before reconciling and welcoming their son, Freddie, in December 2017. Nathan proposed to Cara in July 2018, bringing her back to the place where it all began—the villa, of course—to pop the question.

The duo exchanged vows in June 2019 and welcomed their second child, daughter Delilah, in July 2020.

After coming in second place on UK's second season in 2016, Alex and Olivia got engaged the following year, with Olivia even appearing on an episode of Say Yes to the Dress to find her dream wedding gown.

The season two pair exchanged vows in a September 2018 ceremony, with their wedding process and life as newlyweds being documented for TLC's Olivia and Alex Said Yes and then Olivia and Alex: Happily Ever After.

Alex and Olivia welcomed their son Abel in June 2022 and announced in February 2025 they're expecting Baby No. 2. Daughter Sienna arrived that August.

Dom and Jess proved to be one of the series' strongest love stories, continuing their relationship after he was voted off the show.

UK's season three couple wed in October 2018 and share two children.

Just when viewers were worried all hope was lost for season three fan-favorite Camilla, Jamie entered late in the game and it was clear who he had shown up for. Swoon.

While they ultimately finished in second, Camilla and Jamie have been going strong ever since their first meeting in 2017. The couple married in September 2021 and share three kids: Nell (born in October 2020), Nora (May 2022) and Brodie (May 2024).

The Love Island UK season four contestants may have left the villa together in 2018, but their romance fizzled out not long after returning from Mallorca. They have since gone their separate ways.

Ellie announced in July 2025 that she had gotten engaged to her boyfriend, whose name she has not publicly announced, one year after debuting their relationship.

Months after Dani and Jack were crowned the champions of Love Island season four, they announced their breakup.

"Jack and I have sadly decided to part ways," Dani wrote on Instagram in December 2018. "It's been an incredible six months, and we will always have a place in our hearts for each other, but we've sadly come to the realisation that it's not meant to be long term. We both plan to stay friends.”

They ended up being more than friends and soon rekindled their romance. But by early 2019, they’d split again—with Jack noting on Instagram "sometimes things aren’t meant to be."

"We will always care a lot for each other and have love for each other," he added in an April 2019 post, "and I mean that from the bottom of my heart and I wish her nothing but happiness."

Jack noted he and Dani “really did try to make it work but it unfortunately didn’t and that is life.” Years later, he shared his battle with addiction contributed to their split.

"I have blown more than a million pounds thanks to drugs, booze and gambling," Jack told The Sun in February 2025. "Drugs helped my relationship with Dani fail. I was absent, my priorities were wrong, I wasn’t a great boyfriend. I am determined to change my future."

Meanwhile, Dani has found love with soccer player Jarrod Bowen, whom she wed in May 2025. Together, they share twin girls Summer and Star, who were born in May 2023. Dani is also mom to Santi, the son she welcomed with ex Sammy Kimmence in January 2021.

Lucie and Joe first paired up on day one of season five. But when he was voted out of the villa, she quickly moved on by dating multiple other men (and admitting to having serious feelings for a taken Tommy). #915. Partick Thistle lose SWPL points for amateur player payments

Partick Thistle have dropped from eighth to ninth in the 10-team table

Partick Thistle have been deducted three points and fined Â£6,000 by the Scottish Women's Premier League for making payments to players who were registered as amateurs last season.

Thistle finished sixth last season and the points penalty means they slip one place to second bottom spot, three points behind Spartans, in the current 10-team table.

It follows a hearing on Monday at which the Glasgow club were found to be in breach of rules about making payments to amateur registered players and "submitting incorrect information regarding the submission of the certificate and undertaking document required as part of the membership criteria process".

Half of Thistle's fine is suspended until the end of season.

Thistle had the right of appeal but said on their website that the club "acknowledges and accepts the verdict".

They add: "The circumstances which led to the breach of SWPL player rule 37 and competition rule E31.11 were a result of a failure of internal process, which has since been addressed and resolved so that it can not occur in future.

"The club admitted the breach immediately when brought to our attention.

"We apologise to our fans for the mistake and its consequences."

Bottom side Aberdeen are now only four points behind Thistle.

#914. Meet the youngest top-flight manager in Europe

Jordan Hadaway has been in charge of Llandudno since August 2023; at 18, he was managing Caerwys and a 41-year-old captain; now 25, he has a UEFA A Licence and took the Seasiders back to the Cymru Premier with promotion in 2025/26

Football Journalist @DanLong__

As football has evolved, so have routes into football management.

Once almost exclusively the preserve of former professionals, a playing career is no longer a prerequisite.

That has opened the door to the younger generation. Thirteen managers and head coaches in England's top four divisions are under 40, with Brighton's Fabian Hurzeler the youngest at 33.

But the Cymru Premier - formerly known as the Welsh Premier League - is home to the youngest top-flight manager in Europe.

Last season, Jordan Hadaway guided Llandudno to promotion from the Cymru North. In July, he turned the grand old age of 25.

Hadaway already had the presence of mind to focus on coaching, rather than playing, by 14.

He completed his Level 1 Leaders Award two days after his 16th birthday and was working towards his UEFA B Licence by 18, when he was in charge at Caerwys and working with a 41-year-old captain.

Later, he coached for the Real Madrid Foundation and, in 2024, he passed his A Licence. He counts Nigel Adkins and Robert Earnshaw among those to have helped him along the way.

During his time at Caerwys, Hadaway wrote to Roy Hodgson, who was then in charge of Crystal Palace.

"He was the oldest manager in league football and I was the youngest manager in football, so my college tutor said to me 'Why don't you just write to him?'" he tells Sky Sports.

"I got an email from his personal assistant and he invited me in, but the day I was due to go down, Covid happened. By the time everything opened back up, he had been sacked!

"It was a bit of a nightmare because I really wanted to go and meet him, but I guess things happen for a reason, don't they?"

It is clear his strong work ethic has helped him progress.

"While I was studying at Liverpool Hope University, some days I'd be up at 2.30am or 3am going to work in the bakery for a family friend as they'd lost staff because of Covid," he says.

"I'd stay there until 9.30am, go to a lecture from 11am until 2pm and then I'd coach from maybe 4pm until 9pm. It was a full-on period in my life!"

And it has not slowed down, given he now balances his part-time managerial role with a full-time role as a teacher.

In December 2022, Hadaway left his role as assistant manager at Cefn Druids to become Llandudno U19s manager, as well as the club's head of youth development.

By the start of the 2023/24 season, he had been named interim first-team manager of a club whos squad and staff had been decimated after its artificial playing surface was condemned by the Welsh FA.

"Everyone had walked away and we were two weeks away from starting the season," he recalls.

"The chairman said to me: 'Will you just try and keep us in the league and make sure we have a club? I don't care if we get relegated if that's what has to happen as long as we've got a team and a club at the end of it.'

"Everyone around me, I'll be honest, told me don't take it. My mum even says to me today: 'I can't believe you took that job'.

"But I saw it as an opportunity to go and try and prove people wrong at a very big club in Wales that has an amazing facility and a good fanbase.

"I had the smallest budget in the league by a country mile. I had one player two weeks before the start of the season and no management team. I had to put all that together in two weeks. We were favourites to get relegated, but I never once thought we would.

"We managed to finish 12th out of 16 and we got to a cup final that year. It's quite incredible, really."

Two years later, he took the club one step further.

"My aim was always to be a Welsh Premier League manager by the time I was 27, 28. Did I ever think I was going to get there? No. It's amazing.

"I'm lucky I've had very good players and very good staff that have enabled me to push the club to that standard. It's not all about me, it's about everybody involved.

"I got quite emotional on that afternoon we got promoted. It was an achievement that probably will stick with me and be one of my best forever."

Asked if he has aged beyond his years with the way his career has progressed, Hadaway quips: "Yes - I think my hairline's shown that!

"A lot of people say I'm the oldest 25-year-old they've ever met. I think I am mature, but I'm mature because of the people I've grown up around. The people you spend the most time with have the biggest impact on you."

That maturity is reflected in his attitude towards what comes next.

Many would leap to the conclusion that, if he is doing well at 25 in Wales, a career over the border in England will be on the cards soon.

That may well come to be true, but Hadaway is in no immediate rush.

"Don't get me wrong, I would love to do it [work in the Premier League or EFL]," he adds.

"However, I love my job and I love supporting young people that need the support in school, and I think it would have to be a very good opportunity to take me away from what I'm doing currently. I'm also not naive.

"But I don't think I should get given a chance because I'm the youngest manager in top-flight football - I think I should be given a chance because I'm good enough.

"If we had this interview again in 10 years' time and I was still at Llandudno, I would be happy, because I'm not someone that chases the stars. I'm someone that likes to make sure I'm doing a good job where I'm at and make sure that when I leave, I've left it in a very good place and it's stable."

For someone who has accomplished so much so young, perhaps Hadaway's strength is in knowing there is no need to rush.

#913. Mormon Wives' Jen Affleck Says She's "Not Doing the Best" Amid Divorce

Jen Affleck, who stars on Hulu’s upcoming Nov. 12 series Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, shared insight into her priorities amid her and Zac Affleck’s divorce.

Jen Affleck is swinging into a new chapter.

After filing for divorce from husband Zac Affleck, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star shared insight into how she’s navigating her new normal.

“I'm not doing the best right now,” Jen—who is currently pregnant with her and Zac’s fourth baby—admitted to E! News in an exclusive interview. “I'm just taking one day at a time, and really just focusing on my kids. And obviously, the timing sucks, especially with me being pregnant.”

Nevertheless, she affirmed, “Ultimately, it was the best decision for us.”

And with that right decision bolstering her sails, Jen enjoyed sailing into the new horizon alongside her Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County costars Bobbi Althoff, Aspyn Ovard, Avery Woods, Madison Bontempo, McCall DaPron, Salomé Andrea, Ashleigh Pease and Jordan McClanahan.

For the Dancing With the Stars alum, the timing of filming Orange County made to an experience that was more freeing than her seasons on Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.

“What's funny is there was no reinventing this time,” the 27-year-old admitted. “I just showed up as me. I feel like for the past seven, eight years of my life, I've tried to mold myself into who I think people want to see, whether it be for my marriage or for TV or for the world. And this year was the first time that I really felt like I was reclaiming my identity and who I actually am.”

So, “going into the season, I just poured my heart into it,” she added. “Nothing was storyline; everything was real.”

That meant allowing the cameras to track her difficult chapter as it played out.

“I'm obviously not excited for people to see all the painful parts of the show,” she continued, “but I'm looking forward to people seeing the real, real me—and I guess I'm still trying to figure out who the real me is as well. So, we'll see that unfold in the future.”

As for how Jen showed up to The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, fans can tune in for the premiere on Thursday, November 12 on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+.

While Jen has in large part remained publicly silent on her divorce—though she did share two videos from her and Zac’s relationship, highlighting his less-than-ideal behavior—Zac shared a five-minute video sharing insight into their split.

“This is something we've been talking about for a long time,” he said of their breakup in the Nov. 5 TikTok. “Jen came to me about a year ago, after Dancing With the Stars, and told me she was unhappy and wanted a divorce. And I basically begged her to stay, told her I’d work on things, fix things, become whoever she needed me to be."

It was during this time that Jen became pregnant with their fourth baby, who will join siblings Nora, 5, Luca, 3, and Penelope, 16 months.

And, much like Jen, Zac wants to make sure their children remain his and her priority.

"That's really my priorities," he shared. "I feel like probably the thing that's eating me alive the most is I feel like I failed my kids, and I'm worried that I'm going to cause them damage. And I just hope that we can still give them a normal childhood, but as far as that goes, Jen and I are definitely on the same page of wanting to give them the best the best life we can."

As for why their marriage came to an end, he reflected, “Marriage is hard. Having your marriage in the public is hard. Raising kids is hard. And I think slowly over time we lost that spark."

Meanwhile, for a closer look at where Jen and Zac’s SLOMW: OC costars stand in their love lives, read on. And don’t miss the premiere of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County on Nov. 12.

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff is dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

#911. How Nick Cannon Really Feels About Mariah Carey Prenup

Ten years after Nick Cannon and Mariah Carey finalized their divorce, the  America’s Got Talent alum, who was married to the singer from 2008 to 2016, revealed the details of their prenup.

Boy, if you wanna know whether Nick Cannon and Mariah Carey had a prenup—he’ll tell you.

Ten years after the former couple—who share 15-year-old twins Moroccan and Monroe—finalized their divorce, the former America’s Got Talent host confirmed they “absolutely” signed a prenuptial agreement before tying the knot in 2008.

“Mariah Carey, her entity, her global conglomerate, is gonna make sure she is protected,” Cannon explained during a Nov. 9 appearance on the On Par with Maury Povich podcast. “Had no problem with it whatsoever. And when it was all said and done, I think it protected both of us.”

Although their divorce wasn’t finalized for two years following their 2014 breakup, the 46-year-old—dad to 10 additional children with five different women—said the process felt “easy.”

Nevertheless, it’s not a process Cannon sees himself going through again, as he doesn’t see himself ever getting remarried.

“I think because of some of the natures of, like, unmarrying are not good,” he continued. “And it’s just the process—you don’t realize it takes so long and how draining it is.”

And while divorce “didn’t affect” his friendship with Carey, he saw how divorce creates pressure points in relationships.

“It really could have affected how we handled one another as friends,” he admitted. “I saw the traps of how this could have turned really bad if we didn’t step in and really engage as a family.”

For Cannon, he considered the friendliness that exists between he and Carey an exception when it comes to divorce.

“We handled it so well,” he added. “We handled it out of love. Never heard me say a bad thing about her. Never heard her say a bad thing about me. And we just kind of made it about the kids.”

Meanwhile, Cannon—who is currently in a non-monogamous relationship with Bre Tiesi and Abby De La Rosa—previously went so far to admit that he and Carey might have another shot at romance in the future.

“We belong together,” he quipped to E! News in 2024, going on to say that he would “be stupid” not to get back together with Carey.

As for why the fantasy hasn’t turned into reality? Cannon acknowledged, “She don’t want me.”

For more on Cannon’s family tree, keep reading…

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Brittany gave birth to her third child with Nick on Sept. 23, 2022.

Abby gave birth to a baby girl, her third child with Nick, in November 2022.

Alyssa gave birth to her and Nick's daughter on Dec. 14, 2022.

The model shared an Instagram video showing the Wild 'n Out star helping to deliver their baby. "Our lives are forever changed," she wrote. "Zen is in every breath I take. I know his spirit was with us in the room that morning. I know he is watching down on us. He shows me signs everyday. I will hold onto this memory forever."

She continued, "I will remember the sound of Nicks voice saying 'it's a girl' and the look of everything we've been through flash across his face. I will remember the sound of her crying out with her first breath and feeling her heartbeat against mine. My sweet girl, I got my surprise!! We love you Halo Marie Cannon!"

#910. Sisters in Sweat: how a former Spurs player got 20,000 Indian women into sport

A dinner-party question, a Sunday kickabout and an idea that snowballed. Nine years on, Tanvie Hans and Swetha Subbiah have taken sporting sisterhood to 10 cities

On a breezy evening in 2017, as conversations flowed and so did the drinks at a dinner party, Tanvie Hans was asked an all-too-familiar question at the table: “Hey, can you teach me how to play football?”

For the Indian-born British footballer, who played professionally in England, it was an easy yes.

After a little planning and some back-and-forth messages 17 women – mostly friends and acquaintances – turned up for Hans’ first football lesson on a Sunday morning in the southern Indian metropolis of Bengaluru, eager to discover the joy of the sport.

Nine years on from that impromptu football session, the group has grown into a community of 20,000 women across India. They may not be sisters by blood, but they are the Sisters in Sweat. Co-founded by Hans and the performance coach Swetha Subbiah, Sisters in Sweat is India’s largest women-first sports community, built to help women move more, play more and connect through a variety of sports.

From Chandigarh in the north to Chennai in the south, the initiative now spans 10 Indian cities, with football among its most popular offerings. “It wasn’t something that Swetha and I sat down to plan or even recognised was a gap in the market,” Hans, a former Tottenham and Fulham midfielder, tells Moving the Goalposts.

“But the moment we started these sessions they became successful and the community kept growing organically. That’s when we recognised that we were catering to an audience that is not being catered to in this way. And who better to do it than two women who are experts in the field?”

At Sisters in Sweat, coach-led football sessions are conducted two to three times a week, with participants free to choose between beginner and intermediate sessions, depending on their level of ability. The entry fee starts at about 300 Indian rupees – just under £2.50 – and women of all ages are welcome. You could be trying football for the first time, getting back to it or simply looking for a fun way to stay active.

The format is pretty simple, and the same one Hans and Subbiah used at their first gathering in 2017. The session begins with a quick huddle; everyone introduces themselves and the coach explains what to expect in the next 90 minutes. A warm-up follows before partner or group drills help break the ice within the group, which often features new faces every week. There is music playing in the background to create a celebratory mood and the session ends with a quick and easy 30-minute game of football.

A first-time participant often leaves with a smile, having ticked off a workout while meeting a bunch of strangers who they can now call friends. “You feel like, ‘Oh, I can actually play football and want to get better. I can’t wait to come back for the next session’,” Hans says. “Honestly, just being at the session opens doors for connection. It happens very naturally, and by the end of 90 minutes, you feel you belong here.”

Beyond nurturing new connections, Sisters in Sweat offers women something increasingly rare in India’s densely populated tier 1 cities: access to third spaces where they can show up and move their bodies without fear of judgment or safety concerns. With India’s fitness market projected to grow from $12.3bn (£9.2bn) in 2024 to $23.2bn by 2030 – an 88.6% increase over six years – Sisters in Sweat’s growth and expansion reflect the broader industry trend.

“My cousin, who is from the UK, was actively involved in our Sisters in Sweat sessions while she was in India on holiday. But after she returned to the UK, she wasn’t able to find a community like that,” Subbiah says. “I have heard the same thing from friends in Singapore and other countries. So, I think we, in many ways, have been the first movers to identify this.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

At the heart of Sisters in Sweat’s aim is to fill the gaping hole left by Indian women dropping out of sport, especially after school or college. In the country’s deeply patriarchal social structure, many women are often discouraged from venturing outdoors alone or playing sport recreationally. For many, having the freedom to stay out late at night is a distant dream or a luxury, at best.

“Once a woman leaves her role as a student, she moves on to her next role in life, which is typically becoming a wife,” Subbiah, who has been a Nike coach for over a decade, says. “Then she takes on all the household duties. Add a kid into the mix, and her personal time is minimised.

“There is also immense pressure on a lot of Indian women not to go out or play outdoors because they could catch a tan and look less appealing. A lot of the work we’ve done is to push past these social constructs and say, “Get a tan, it’s beautiful. Come out and play with us, you’ll feel great.”

#909. Manchester City’s Kerstin Casparij: ‘I love football – but it takes over your life’

Dutch full-back on relief of winning the Double and needing a ‘sense of normality’ while in the spotlight

Kerstin Casparij loves football, especially Champions League nights under the lights, but perspective is important too. “I would say football is my most important secondary thing in life, and I’ve found that such a refreshing way of looking at it,” she says before Manchester City’s trip to Milan to face Inter on Tuesday.

“It is so important to me and I love it so much and if I lose I’m going to have a terrible day, but my family’s healthy, my friends are healthy, I am, and I don’t have to worry about anything; I don’t have to worry about getting the food on the table. Being able to see things from that perspective makes it so much easier to stay the person I’ve always been.”

The 26-year-old Dutch full-back has had a phenomenal year, winning a first league title and FA Cup with Manchester City in her fourth season in England. Casparij was integral, having arguably her best season in the Women’s Super League, scoring three times and providing seven assists – the joint-most assists in the league with Aston Villa’s Lynn Wilms.

Key to her growth last season under Andrée Jeglertz was that “now I’m allowed to really play on almost the whole right side”, she says. “And I’m allowed to and trusted with pushing forward and taking risks in the final third.”

Like all team players, Casparij credits her teammates, but her contribution was recognised with a place on the Ballon d’Or shortlist. She finished in 24th place, the fifth-highest defender.

Being able to share these wins with her team outside the team is important too. They “work tirelessly to help me out”, she says. “Especially my partner, who is so invested in my career and has been such an incredible support and helped me out in more ways than I can count. There are so many incredible people around me and I’m just really happy I can give back to them as well, as much as I’m proud of myself for achieving it.”

Casparij’s authenticity, openness and playfulness have made her a fan favourite, not only at City but across the league. Her pun-loaded Instagram captions are as witty and self-critical after a defeat as they are sharp when City win. She is funny, shows fire on the pitch and is not afraid of banter with rivals, and is also a passionate advocate for the causes that matter to her, including as an LGBT Foundation patron and by sharing her experiences growing up with ADHD. Social media is a key tool for connecting.

“I always want to be me and I want people that I knew 10 years ago to now speak to me and be able to be like: ‘Oh you haven’t changed a single bit, you’re still the same person.’ I have a lot of friends outside of football and it gives you such a sense of normality because football, the industry, is not normal and we are not necessarily normal.”

The connection with people matters because it cuts through the abnormality. “We’re in the spotlight every three days at times. We’re getting judged on our performance, we’re getting judged on how we do our work, so I kind of need that sense of normality to make sure I don’t take things too seriously and really keep both my feet on the ground.”

Having a partner who isn’t fazed by what comes with being a professional football player and understands the schedule and lifestyle is a big part of that. “I absolutely love football, I love everything about it, but it takes over your life and it’s definitely taken over ours,” she says. “You need a partner that understands that and loves it and is like: ‘Yeah, let’s do this together.’

“I’m so grateful for her and am so appreciative of her. She’s got weekends off but she doesn’t really have weekends off because they all revolve around me. Life revolves around me a lot and I try to make extra effort to make sure she knows it’s about her, too. We’re definitely a two-person team here, but to have her support and know she’s always there, she’s a massive part of my football journey.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

That journey has taken her a long way from Heerenveen, for whom she made her debut at 15. Almost two years ago, when Casparij signed a new long-term City contract, she told the Guardian she felt she had unfinished business at the club. She wanted to win, so what did securing the Double in May feel like? “Incredible. It was such a long time coming and I’d been dreaming of that for so long.

“There was a big feeling of relief. We were very determined to win the league and I feel like we remained very calm for very, very long, pretty much up until the end. We just knew what we needed to do to get the job done and we made a big point of having a winning language. As a leadership team we started to talk about ‘when’ we win the league rather than ‘if’ to create an environment that believed and where everyone was going to do everything we could to win.”

Whether City can retain their title is the big question. They did not play in the Champions League last season and there were questions before this campaign over whether they could juggle the workload. After nine games they are top and unbeaten, two points clear of Chelsea, who drew 1-1 with Everton at the weekend, before their meeting on Saturday at Stamford Bridge. City look as formidable as ever in attack but earned only their second clean sheet in their 5-0 defeat of West Ham on Saturday. In the Champions League, they have three draws from three games as they get reacquainted with the demands of European competition.

Were they aware of the doubts some had in pre-season? “Late last season some were still thinking we were going to bottle it,” Casparij says with a smile. “We see it. I’m not going to say we don’t, because we all follow the media, we all have social media, but it’s not something that gets really discussed very heavily. But it definitely adds fuel to our fire …

“It also allows us, as a team, to keep innovating, to keep thinking: ‘OK, what can we change? What can we improve? Where can we get better? Where do we sometimes need to tweak little things? What does the opponent do?’ And that’s the beauty of it and the fun part because it never gets boring.”

#908. Lecturer's bid to challenge Fifa president Infantino

Peter Auf der Heyde reveals his motives behind trying to run for the Fifa presidency

University lecturer Peter Auf der Heyde is launching an ambitious attempt to take on Gianni Infantino for the Fifa presidency.

The former journalist and football club owner is seeking to be nominated to challenge the incumbent Infantino - and wants to be paid a salary of just $1 (75p) per year if he wins the role.

South African Auf der Heyde lectures in journalism at Southampton Solent University and was previously sports editor of the Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa) in Germany.

He was president of the Grahamstown Soccer Association in South Africa and both owned and managed second-division side UDW FC in the early 1990s.

"I feel very strongly that there needs to be a challenge in any election," Auf der Heyde told BBC Radio Solent.

"There should not be an uncontested election and in this case Infantino needs to be challenged. It's important for accountability and transparency."

For Auf der Heyde to become a candidate to challenge Infantino in the March 2027 election, he will need to be nominated by five football associations.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is also considering standing against the current president, who faced calls to stand down following a controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Infantino insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, and laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning his position.

He is seeking a fourth and final term in the role but is also facing competition from Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association, and former Tottenham Hotspur and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November.

"I'm not asking for countries to vote for me, I'm asking for them to nominate me," added Auf der Heyde.

"Once you have a nomination and become an official candidate you can then ask questions [to other candidates] that you can't ask otherwise.

"Infantino earned around $6m (Â£4.49m) last year which I think is ridiculous. I would suggest that $450,000 (Â£337,259) is a very adequate salary and in my case I would ask to be paid $1 per year and after four years if I have maintained my promises then I can get the remaining money."

Wenger considers standing against Infantino

Auf der Heyde revealed that so far he has written to all 211 of Fifa's member associations, with replies already from the Jamaican and English Football Associations.

He broke down his manifesto for the role into three sections, with a key part of that being a new global competition for smaller footballing nations.

Only 48 nations qualify for the men's World Cup finals every four years with 163 missing out.

"I'd like to see an emerging nations World Cup," said Auf der Heyde, who covered 13 consecutive Africa Cup of Nations as a journalist.

"This would be for countries like Eswatini, Andorra and San Marino, who will quite frankly never qualify for the World Cup.

"They should be allowed in my view to play for a global competition where only these kind of countries have a chance to play.

"It would be wonderful if winning teams from that competition could then qualify further for the World Cup."
