#884. Felix Nmecha denies goal celebrations promote ‘intolerance, discrimination and hate’

Celebrations linked to ultra-conservative Christian group

‘Our message is of love’ Nmecha says in reply to criticism

The Borussia Dortmund and Germany midfielder Felix Nmecha has responded to criticism of goal celebrations linked to an evangelical network by saying they have been misunderstood and are not meant to promote “intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form”.

Nmecha, a devout Christian, was criticised by the Dortmund official supporters’ group at the weekend for celebrating goals with a gesture signifying the “The King’s Return” campaign linked to Ballers in God (BIG), a network of Christian football players. The German public broadcaster ARD has linked BIG to ultra-conservative positions on issues including homosexuality and transgender identity.

“My celebration is not intended to promote myself or any organisation,” Nmecha wrote in a social media post on Tuesday. “Rather, it is about laying my ‘crown’ before the soon coming King and pointing to Jesus, my hope and strength. My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form.

“As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for everyone, regardless of where they come from, what they believe, or what their worldview may be.”

In a statement, Dortmund official supporters’ group said: “We oppose religious networks that, under the guise of faith, propagate a worldview in which individuals are denigrated or excluded based on their sexual orientation, gender identity, way of life, or personal choices”.

Dortmund said on Sunday that it understood the fans’ concerns and would speak to Nmecha. “For Borussia Dortmund, it is essential to take the concerns and needs of the fanbase seriously and to address them,” read a statement. “Naturally, we also take the current media coverage and the associated questions and discussions very seriously.”

The news agency DPA reported that Jürgen Klopp, Germany’s head coach, has already spoken to Nmecha about the issue at the national team camp in Herzogenaurach, Bavaria, before the upcoming Nations League games.

#882. The fans at the foggy FA Cup game no-one could see

Ian Kirke struggled to watch his side's FA Cup first round match against Altrincham due to thick fog

For many football fans, an FA Cup win is the stuff of dreams. But for 690 Notts County supporters, thick fog meant they could barely see it happen.

Ian Kirke was among the Magpies fans whose view of Saturday's FA Cup first-round tie against Altrincham was obscured by fog, leaving many unable to see the League One side's penalty shootout victory.

The thick layer of fog provided chaos not just for the players and fans, but also commentators and camera operators at the J Davidson Stadium.

Kirke said fans had to rely on the cheers - or silence - from the home support during the shootout. "It's the most bonkers festival of football I've ever seen in my life," he added.

Heavy fog meant Notts County fans were unable to watch the penalty shootout that took place at the other end of the pitch

Lifelong fan Kirke, who lives in Berkshire, said the weather at kick-off was "like any normal match".

Before fog descended over Greater Manchester, Jacob Bedeau had given Notts County the lead just before the half-hour mark.

The hosts, who play in the National League, hit back as Lucas Weaver and Lewis Banks scored to give Altrincham a 2-1 lead.

With the conditions worsening, referee David Rock opted to continue with the tie, which saw the camera often unable to pick up the ball.

The referee's decision to continue the game paid off for Notts County, who levelled the tie at 2-2, when Callum Roberts scored from the edge of the box.

"It's like a fever dream" - commentators struggle through fog

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard was also commentating on BBC Radio Nottingham, and said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot the ball competition.

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Lynda Lally said the fog got worse during the second half

Fellow Magpies fan Lynda Lally, from Beeston in Nottinghamshire, said the weather got "worse and worse" after half-time.

"For the other 45 minutes, we could only see what was happening once players emerged from the fog," she said.

The weather became "a cross between an eerie Christmas nativity gone horribly wrong - and the 1980s film called The Fog," Kirke said.

Kirke added the fog that led to an FA Cup third-round replay between Notts County and Wimbledon being abandoned in 2001 "wasn't as bad" as it was at Altrincham.

"I don't know what on earth had to happen for the referee to call it off," he said.

With the game going to penalties, Lally had hoped the shootout would take place in front of the Notts County fans so she could finally see the ball.

"Once we found out it wasn't, we were thinking what is going to happen because we can't see anything," she said.

"There was a deathly silence amongst the Notts fans when Altrincham fans at the other end were excited, and when they went silent, we went wild."

Kirke said his friend, who was struggling to see the action on TV, texted him updates during the penalty shootout.

"The only way we could ascertain what was going on was the reaction of the Altrincham fans," he said.

The sound of disappointment echoed around the stadium as Altrincham missed the target three times, before Rosaire Longelo slotted home the decisive penalty to seal a 3-2 shootout victory for Notts County.

"We heard the silence and we went into a massive roar knowing we had won," Lally added.

#880. Rui Pinto’s lawyers in talks with UK authorities over deal for Manchester City whistleblower

He is willing to assist in exchange for protection

Rui Pinto’s lawyers are in talks with British authorities over a potential cooperation agreement under which the Manchester City whistleblower could help to expose serious financial and sporting crime in the UK.

According to information obtained by the Guardian, the Serious Fraud Office has contacted Pinto after it emerged he was willing to assist British authorities with their investigations in exchange for protection.

William Bourdon, Pinto’s lawyer, who has represented whistleblowers such as Edward Snowden and Julian Assange, told the Guardian that contact had been established. “I can confirm that the process is under way,” he said, without providing further details.

If an agreement is reached, the Football Leaks founder could become a significant source of information in investigations into financial crime involving football, law firms and powerful business figures. Between 2015 and 2019, Pinto collected tens of millions of files containing sensitive information. He may be able to assist the SFO in identifying potential tax offences and other irregularities that would otherwise have gone undetected.

The development comes at a significant moment for the 38-year-old Pinto, with his future under Portugal’s witness protection programme uncertain.

Pinto rose to prominence by exposing some of the football industry’s most closely guarded secrets. These included Cristiano Ronaldo’s tax affairs, plans by Europe’s leading clubs to establish a breakaway European Super League and a series of controversial financial arrangements. His revelations triggered investigations and contributed to legal proceedings involving clubs and players across several countries.

More recently, documents collected and leaked by the whistleblower became relevant to the Premier League’s investigation into Manchester City, which resulted in the club being found in breach of financial rules.

The information gathered by Pinto is in the possession of French authorities, who sought previously to include him in a witness protection programme. His arrest by Portuguese police in Hungary in January 2019 disrupted those plans, although France has maintained contact with him. Between his arrest in Hungary and his extradition to Portugal, French authorities travelled to Budapest and copied the contents of the electronic devices in his possession.

Pinto was informed on 30 September, just as his name had made headlines again after the City ruling, that he would no longer be protected by the Portuguese authorities after six years under the witness protection programme. Although the authorities maintained there was no threat to his life, he was advised not to express opinions on controversial issues, to avoid crowded places and to limit the time spent with family members.

The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action

Pinto was given 10 days’ warning, even though a decision had been taken in July, and the ruling’s implementation was suspended after it was established that he had not been given an opportunity to mount a challenge or appeal. He then appealed and is awaiting a final ruling.

In 2023 Pinto was given a suspended four-year prison sentence in Portugal for attempted extortion and cybercrime offences. He was acquitted in a second case involving similar charges two years later. The public prosecutor’s office and Benfica, one of the clubs hacked by Pinto, appealed against the ruling. A decision from the higher court is awaited.

Supporters regard Pinto as a whistleblower who cast light on corruption, whereas detractors argue that his tactics breached legal standards and moral principles. His disclosures reached far beyond football. Details involving magistrates, legal professionals and public officials were made public and he was the whistleblower behind Luanda Leaks, which exposed the inner workings of the business empire of Africa’s richest woman, Isabel dos Santos. She denied corruption allegations.

#879. McTominay reveals he had heart ‘shocked’ two days before World Cup opener

Midfielder was in hospital before Scotland v Haiti

‘I had to get the shock on my heart,’ says McTominay

Scott McTominay has revealed he was in hospital under sedation to have a “shock on my heart” just 48 hours before Scotland began their World Cup campaign against Haiti in June.

At the time McTominay’s absence from training was put down to a stomach complaint. It emerged in August that the Napoli midfielder needed surgery to remedy an irregular heartbeat. The operation took place in September, causing McTominay to miss Scotland’s first four Nations League matches. The player has now said the matter arose in the US as Scotland prepared for their World Cup opener at Boston Stadium.

McTominay is back in the international fold for Scotland’s fixtures against North Macedonia and Switzerland. Talking to media in Glasgow the 29-year-old said: “The World Cup was difficult for me to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. It was two days before the Haiti game and you have prepared so well. I was in such good condition and then something like that happens. And you think: ‘How is this happening to me?’ But then you have to get on with it.

“These are cards you are dealt in football. Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say it’s part of the process.

“Whenever you are sitting in a hospital bed two days before the first game at the World Cup, about to get put to sleep it’s not ideal is it? When things like that happen it is what it is, there’s nothing you can do about it. After the World Cup I reflected on it and it’s probably the most disappointed I have been in my career.”

Sébastien Pocognoli, Clarke’s successor, will call on McTominay for the first time when North Macedonia visit Hampden Park on Friday. McTom­inay returned to the Napoli team in early October. “I’m feeling much, much better than what I was,” said McTominay. “It [the operation] was something that needed to be done. In your career you have moments like that, where things can take you by surprise. It looks a lot worse to people in the media and family or friends who reach out to you when they see news relating to a heart issue, but it was a relatively straightforward procedure which went really, really well in Manchester. I’m really happy to be back and playing football again.

“It was explained to me really well by the doctors at Napoli and my cardiologist in Manchester so the process was really straightforward. The doctor with Scotland when we were away at the World Cup explained, if that was going to be the case how it would look. All the staff members made me feel so relaxed about the situation.”

Ryan Phillippe, already dad to two adult kids with Reese Witherspoon and a teen daughter with ex Alexis Knapp, shared how time with a baby relative has left him with some serious “baby fever.”

Ryan Phillippe knows what he’s doing next summer—and it doesn’t involve changing diapers.

Though the Cruel Intentions star’s three kids have reached a more independent stage of life—he and ex-wife Reese Witherspoon share Ava, 27, and Deacon, 23, while he’s also dad to daughter Kai, 15, with ex Alexis Knapp—time with younger relatives has left him wishing for another chapter of parenthood.

“Good morning from Uncle Philz & baby Elkie,” Phillippe, 52, wrote on Instagram Nov. 10 alongside a picture of himself holding the youngster poolside. “I really do be having baby fever.”

However, the I Know What You Did Last Summer alum admitted that is likely not in the cards as he currently has “no woman” and believes he’s “too old.”

But it comes as no surprise that Phillippe would be down to continue growing his family. After all, he’s been vocal about how intentional he’s been about raising his kids.

“Well, you hope that while they're young and they are in the same house as you, that you instill enough of the values and the sensibilities that they'll need when they go out into the world,” he told Scary Mommy in February. “As a parent, you're always there for them and trying to guide and give them advice, but there has to be an element of release once they get over a certain age.”

And now that Phillippe is watching his eldest kids move through the world on their own, he confirmed, “I feel good and proud of who they are and how myself and my ex-wife have prepared them.”

Plus, the 9-1-1 Nashville actor is glad to see Ava and Deacon follow in his and Witherspoon’s acting footsteps, because as he previously put it, “What makes me proudest is seeing all three of my kids success and achieve.”

"I'm wanting and hoping that they have happy and well-balanced lives," he told People in May 2025. "That's where the biggest source of pride in my life comes from: seeing them achieve and be good people."

#874. Hussain calls 'Sandpapergate' affair a 'complete mess'

Michael Atherton says Cricket Australia "left questions unanswered" with initial handling of incident eight years ago and that the players "not having each other's backs" will cause most "disquiet" among fans; Australia play England in eight white-ball matches from Friday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports' Nasser Hussain has called the Australia 'Sandpapergate' affair and its subsequent explosive fallout a "complete mess".

The 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa, in which Australia's Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera trying to use sandpaper on the ball in order to make it swing, has been catapulted back into the spotlight following the release of Usman Khawaja's book.

Former Baggy Greens batter Khawaja, who played in that infamous Cape Town Test, claims the entire team knew about the scheme and not just those banned, in Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and David Warner, who was deemed the architect.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Khawaja also said he was not quizzed at the time by Cricket Australia despite sitting next to Bancroft in the Newlands dressing room and that he urged the team to come clean and take collective responsibility before being talked out of it by Smith.

Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, former England captain Hussain said: "I think it's a complete mess.

"Let's be honest, for the history of the game, people have been trying to work out what to do with cricket balls to make it swing more, whether it be mints, sweets, throwing the ball to the ground on the bounce, Vaseline, dirt in pocket, whatever it might be.

"[But] how a side thought it was okay to take sandpaper out, how no one before that in a meeting went, 'I don't think this is okay, I don't think we're doing the right thing', how they thought they were going to get away with it with all the cameras around [I don't know].

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Then to lie about it after and for Cricket Australia not to speak to every player, not to speak to Khawaja who was sitting next to Bancroft. It just feels like a right mess.

"The team, the baggy green, the mateship and all that stuff - that was what playing Australia was like, so for an Australian team to say, 'no, it's just those three' when it was never going to be just those three [is surprising]."

Hussain's fellow analyst, Michael Atherton, is currently in Australia ahead of England's white-ball tour of the country, which begins with the first ODI in Perth on Friday (3.30am UK time).

Atherton will attend what he anticipates being a "circus" of a press conference on Thursday as Australia white-ball captain Mitchell Marsh - the only player to have figured in the Newlands Test in 2018 in the hosts' squad to tackle England - fronts up.

Usual ODI skipper Pat Cummins has been rested, along with Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, all three of whom were involved in the sandpaper Test and released a joint statement back in 2021, with spinner Nathan Lyon, denying prior knowledge of the plot.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports pundit Atherton was critical of Cricket Australia's handling of the situation eight years ago, saying it was always "going to come back to haunt them".

Smith and Warrner were banned for a year after 'Sandpapergate' with Bancroft suspended for nine months.

Atherton, who does not see a need for a new investigation to be opened following Khawaja's claims, said: "It was almost like the sandpaper was the straw that broke the camel's back.

"It was on the back of the team having become, and Khawaja talks about it in his book, slightly out of control, a bit unlikable and with a kind of win-at-all costs mentality.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"They handed down unbelievably heavy sanctions - I thought hard-to-justify sanctions - and left three players to take the rap. But it left questions unanswered, left the door open for it to come back to haunt them, which it is doing now.

"It was eight years ago and there will be a weariness around the story eventually, because it's all over every newspaper, podcast, whatever.

"But I do think the particular point about not having people's backs is the thing causing the most disquiet [in the Australia public] and will rumble on for a while yet."

Australia have also toiled on the field, losing 2-1 in South Africa in their first Test series in the country since the ball-tampering scandal, with the out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne now dropped for the impending home clashes with New Zealand.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Amid a relentless Test calendar that then features a five-match assignment in India, the day-night 150th anniversary Test against England in Melbourne in March, and an away Ashes series in June and July, Atherton feels the Baggy Greens are in a tough spot.

He added: "The schedule is brutal and unforgiving and already there's cracks in that team.

"It doesn't feel as though the team is robust enough to get through this period.

"This [the ball-tampering claims] is adding a little bit more fuel to the fire."

Listen to Nasser Hussain, Michael Atherton and guests dissect the game's big talking points.

#873. Christina Applegate Thinks Breast Implants Are Making Her Sick

After Christina Applegate shared she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, she questioned if her breast implants could be the cause of her health issues.

Christina Applegate is still on a quest for answers.

Weeks after the Married…With Children alum shared that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, she began questioning if the breast implants she received after her 2008 breast cancer diagnosis could be causing her health issues.

“I’ve been thinking this for years,” Applegate shared with her MeSsy podcast host Jamie-Lynn Sigler on the Nov. 10 episode. “Is the breast implant poisoning? Because I actually had my double mastectomy in 2008 and I am way overdue for having them replaced.”

The 54-year-old added, “I swear, over the last five years or whatever, I thought, ‘What if it's seriously, what if they're leaking and they're poisoning me?’”

Her thoughts on the matter were also amplified after reading a study about breast implant poisoning “presenting as MS.”

“So that's one that I will be looking into,” Applegate noted, “because it's something I've thought about.”

The Dead to Me actress—who shares 15-year-old daughter Sadie with husband Martyn LeNoble—has been candid about her health struggles since she first shared her MS diagnosis in 2021. However, now that she’s learned she was misdiagnosed, she’s struggling to find out what is actually causing her issues.

"This may come as great news,” she said on the Oct. 20 episode of MeSsy, “but to me it comes as, like, I'm back at square one.”

That’s why when her doctor "came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,’” Applegate recalled, "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."

She also felt particularly discouraged as she explained to Sigler that she hasn’t “gotten better,” adding,  "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me."

And she knew it would be hard for doctors to pinpoint a new diagnosis as she has “every symptom of someone with MS,” noting that there are many illnesses that can mirror MS.

Still, despite not having the disease, she shared that she was grateful to the MS community and continues to feel a part of it, despite her misdiagnosis.

“You guys are my people,” Applegate said on MeSsy Oct. 27. “Even though I don’t have this disease, I have fallen in love with everyone that we know—listeners and our friends—that have MS and I’m still your warrior.”

“I’m still going to speak out on your behalf for ever and ever,” she assured. “I still feel like part of this community. No matter what, I love you.”

For a look at Applegate’s health journey over the years, keep reading.

Christina Applegate shared she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021.

"Hi friends. A few months ago I was diagnosed with MS," she shared on her social media channels that August. "It's been a strange journey. But I have been so supported by people that I know who also have this condition. It's been a tough road. But as we all know, the road keeps going. Unless some a--hole blocks it."

"Oh, by the way, I have a disease," she joked during her November 2022 Hollywood Walk of Fame induction ceremony, her first public appearance since her MS diagnosis. "Did you not notice? I'm not even wearing shoes."

Applegate believes her MS journey actually began "six or seven years" before her 2021 diagnosis.

"I noticed, especially the first season [of Dead to Me], we'd be shooting and my leg would buckle," Applegate explained during a March 2024 interview on Good Morning America. "I really just put it off as being tired, or I'm dehydrated, or it's the weather. Then nothing would happen for months, and I didn't pay attention."

By the time she was shooting the Netflix series' third and final season, the actress said she was "being brought to set in a wheelchair."

"I couldn't move that far," she recalled, "so I had to tell everybody because I needed help."

The Dead to Me star captioned this photo of her cane collection amid her battle with MS: "Walking sticks are now part of my new normal."

Joined by her daughter Sadie Grace LeNoble, Applegate had a simple message for multiple sclerosis while attending the 2023 SAG Awards: "F U MS."

And she's not the only one experiencing strong feelings towards the illness. "In my situation, Sadie only knew me as healthy and a runner and a Pelotoner and a dancer—and she only knew that," Applegate explained to friend Jamie-Lynn Sigler on an August 2025 episode of their MeSsy podcast. "So then when this came about in 2021, she was, like, stoic about it."

Yet, "I see her look at me when I’m in bed," Applegate continued, "and can't quite move or, I want to go say goodnight to her in her room but I can’t quite get down the hallway for whatever reason my legs aren’t working that day."

The whole experience has "broken" her teen, Applegate noted. "It was like losing the mom she had to this f--king thing. And the more she’s gotten older now, I think the more it’s hurting her."

After a receiving standing ovation at the 2023 Emmys, the Married...With Children alum quipped, "You're totally shaming me with disability by standing up."

"I make these jokes because if I don't, I'll suffocate," Applegate shared on a March 2024 episode on Armchair Expert, explaining why she often pokes fun at her condition. "I'll be done."

So, yes, she's going to talk about the fact that she's already purchased burial plots.

"My friend and I are going to go take a picnic there," Applegate revealed on a March 2026 episode of NPR's Wild Card. "It's really pretty where it is." She just has to pick out a tree "'cause it's really sunny," she continued. "And I want my visitors to not be sweating."

"I have 30 lesions on my brain," she noted on Armchair Expert. "My biggest one is behind my right eye, so my right eye hurts a lot."

Legions are caused by the immune system attacking the myelin sheath around nerves, according to the Multiple Sclerosis Trust.

Applegate hasn’t held back when it comes to sharing her journey.

"It sucks," the Anchorman actress told late night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel of her daily struggles with MS. "I'm not going to lie. I think anyone who has MS isn't going to be like, 'This is the best thing that ever happened to me!'"

Besides, she'd taken that tack when discussing her breast cancer battle back in 2008. "I went out, and I was the good girl talking about 'Oh, I love my new boobs' that are all scarred and f--ked up. What was I thinking?" she said on Armchair Expert. "Everything I was saying was a freaking lie. It was me trying to convince myself of something, and I think that did no service to anyone."

While she started a foundation and "raised millions of dollars for women to get MRIs who were at high risk," she noted, "at the back of it, I was taking off my bra and crying every night. And I wish that I had said that."

When talking about her day-to-day life with the disease, Applegate told Good Morning America in March 2024, "I live kind of in hell."

"But I might get to a place where I function a little bit better," she added. "Right now, I'm isolating, and that's kind of how I'm dealing with it—by not going anywhere because I don't want to do it. It's hard."

Christina credited her Sweetest Thing costar Selma Blair—who was diagnosed with MS in 2018—for urging her to get tested for the disease.

"She said, 'You need to get checked for MS,'" Christina recalled during her GMA interview. "If not for her, it could've been way worse."

Applegate confirmed that Dead to Me will likely be her last onscreen credit, telling Vanity Fair in May 2023, "I can’t even imagine going to set right now."

"I’m probably not going to work on-camera again, but I'm so glad that I went out with someone who is by far the greatest actress I’ve ever worked with in my entire life," she said of costar Linda Cardellini, "if not the greatest human I’ve ever known.

For Applegate, contracting sapovirus—a virus commonly transmitted through fecal-oral contact—meant having to rely on adult diapers.

"I woke up at three o'clock in the morning in a pool of s--t," she explained on an April 2024 episode of her MeSsy podcast. "I didn't know what happened, and having MS at three o'clock in the morning and trying to change your sheets, it's not fun. But this brings me to my next point, which we can talk about: I'm wearing diapers."

Their discussion was "so liberating," her co-host Sigler noted. "This is something you do by yourself and it feels terrible when you're doing it. I've done that hundreds of times in my MS journey through the years when I've experienced a flair or when I was sick."

"I am in a depression right now, which I don't think I've felt for years," Applegate confessed to Sigler on another 2024 episode of their MeSsy podcast. "Like a real, f--k it all, like real depression where it's kind of scaring me too a little bit because it feels really fatalistic."

Three years into her diagnosis, she continued, "And I'm still sitting here like ‘Boohoo, woe is me.' I'm still mad about it." But the truth was, added, "I don't enjoy living—I don't enjoy things anymore."

Applegate acknowledged the reality of living with MS can be grim. “Everybody has different ways of it showing up,” she noted on a November 2024 episode of her podcast. "I lay in bed screaming. Like, the sharp pains, the ache, the squeezing."

At times, the discomfort even makes it hard for her to enjoy her one source of comfort, the reality TV that at times is "on 24/7 in my room," she noted. But, "I can’t even pick up my phone sometimes," Applegate added, "because now it’s traveled into my hands. So I’ll try to go get my phone or get my remote to turn on the TV or whatever, and sometimes I can’t even hold them."

Since her 2021 diagnosis, Applegate has gotten used to the feel of an open-front gown. "I've been in the hospital upwards of 30 times from throwing up and diarrhea and pain," she relayed on her pocast in March 2025. "That is unimaginable, OK? They’ve done every test known to man on me, put so much radiation into my body from CT scans to everything else."

In the plus column, she noted, she has connected some of her gastro issues to her larger illness. "I have noticed that—and I’m going to be really honest—if I have to poop, I puke," she detailed. "And when I puke, I get all the pain and then all the things happen."

Mere months after her hospital confession, Applegate was checking back in. Returning from a family trip to Europe, "I'm like, 'I wanna be admitted. I'm staying here because I want answers,'" she recounted that August of what she told staff. "'I want every test that you can possibly think of or ones that you haven't even thought of, and I want them done.'"

Following a middle-of-the-night CT, she learned, "I had kidney infections."

More than five years after sharing her battle with multiple sclerosis, she learned that she was misdiagnosed.

"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,'" she recalled of her doctor's visit in the October 2026 podcast MeSsy. "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."

Applegate emphasized that the confirmation of the misdiagnosis hadn't changed how she's continued to struggle physically.

"I haven't gotten better," she said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. That's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021."

#871. Wales call up MK Dons' Collins as Moore withdraws

Aaron Collins (right) has seven goals in the past three games for MK Dons and is the EFL's joint-top goalscorer

Wales have called up uncapped MK Dons striker Aaron Collins for this month's Nations League matches following Wrexham frontman Kieffer Moore's withdrawal due to injury.

Moore, 34, left the field during Wrexham's 1-1 Championship draw with Wolves on Saturday.

Wales have not specified what kind of injury the 57-cap forward has sustained.

He is replaced in the Wales squad by Collins, who has scored 17 goals in 16 games across all competitions for League One side Dons this season, including four goals in a game against Doncaster last month.

The 29-year-old former Newport County player joins Craig Bellamy's squad for concluding Group A4 games in Norway and at home to Portugal.

Newport-born Collins has played for 10 different - mainly lower league - clubs since leaving Rodney Parade for Wolverhampton Wanderers in 2016.

Wales, who are looking to preserve their place in the Nations League's top tier, face Norway in Oslo on Saturday before finishing their campaign at home against Portugal next Tuesday.

Wales are third in Group A4, with their only win from four matches so far coming against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway in Cardiff last month.

Bellamy is without midfielder Jordan James but has influential Leeds pair Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon back, along with Cardiff playmaker Rubin Colwill.

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Bellamy's side could still finish in second, third or fourth place.

A top-two spot would take Wales to the Nations League quarter-finals in March 2027.

Finishing third would mean a relegation play-off against a League B team in March, while finishing bottom of the group would result in either a relegation play-off or direct relegation, depending on the ranking with other League A groups.

#869. Why Joshua Jackson Was Only Dawson's Creek Star Missing From Memoir

In Kerr Smith’s new memoir I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek, Joshua Jackson was not interviewed like this fellow cast—and Smith shared why in an exclusive E! News interview.

Kerr Smith didn’t want to wait to tell his Dawson’s Creek story.

And so, fans of The WB series might notice that while Katie Holmes, Michelle Williams and James Van Der Beek sat for interviews for his new memoir I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek, Joshua Jackson did not return to Capeside—and that wasn’t Smith’s decision.

“All I want to say is everybody makes a choice about whether or not they want to be part of the project or not,” Smith told E! News in an exclusive interview. “Some did, some didn't.”

And Smith appeared to nod to Jackson’s hesitation to participate in a parenthetical within the book itself, which hit shelves today, Nov. 10, while recounting that scene between Holmes’ Joey and Jackson’s Pacey in the series finale.

While pushing back on Holmes’ admission that she didn’t love her performance, Smith revealed Jackson wasn’t available to share his perspective.

“Allow me to weigh in with my expert analysis. (Yep, I’m now an expert. I mean, have you not heard? I wrote the book on this stuff.),” Smith wrote. “With all due respect, you’re wrong. You positively crushed this scene. Both of you. Right, Josh? Josh? (I’m sure he’ll get back to me any second now.)”

E! News reached out to Jackson’s rep for comment but hasn’t heard back.

But while Smith and Jackson didn’t go down memory lane, or rather creek, together, the Final Destination alum emphasized what it meant to him to revisit series with the rest of the cast and crew.

“I wanted to get everybody else’s memory on it too,” Smith told E!. “I did over two dozen interviews for the book so I wanted to get everybody’s experiences and put it in one place to understand what a great show this is.”

When it came to his conversations with Holmes, the 54-year-old mused that it was easy for them to simply snap right back into the late 1990s, adding, “It’s like we never even lost a step.”

“You make those bonds back then and you just kind of hang on to them,” he added. “It doesn’t matter how many years have gone by.”

And, of course, it was especially sentimental for Smith to get to reminisce with Van Der Beek before his death earlier this year after a three-year battle with colorectal cancer.

“When I did interview James, he was already pretty sick,” Smith noted. “But he was kind enough to give me a few hours and we had an amazing discussion.”

In addition to being a reflection on Dawson’s Creek as a whole, Smith also included a chapter for former cast and crew to share their memories with Van Der Beek following his death.

“I wanted to give everybody that knew him back then a chance to say anything at all if they wanted to,” Smith shared. “I just thought it was really nice. I think it’s something that he would’ve been OK with.”

As he put it, “I think it’s a good way to end the story.”

You can read the entire fantastic, Steven Spielberg-film worthy story in Smith’s new memoir, and keep reading for even more secrets into the beloved teen drama…

While Fox was first to pick up Dawson's Creek, it subsequently dumped the teen drama.

"I was told they were struggling with Party of Five and they didn't need another one," series creator Kevin Williamson said at the 2015 ATX TV Festival.

But that paved the way for The WB to pick it up two years later.

While Paula Cole's "I Don't Want to Wait" became the iconic Dawson's Creek theme song, producers originally wanted Alanis Morissette's "Hand in My Pocket."

Alas, they couldn't land the rights, what a jagged little pill.

Dawson. Pacey. Joey. Not names you hear every day. So how did Williamson come up with them?

"Dawson came from a real place called Dawson's Creek where we all hung out as kids and partied," he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018, while Pacey "came from a friend of a friend named Pacey and I'd never met anyone with that name and thought it was a cool name."

And for the show's heroine, Williamson "wanted Josephine as a very girly name that could easily turn into a tomboy name like Joey."

Remember Dawson's infamous "walk the dog" line in the pilot?

Williamson inserted the euphemism because the network would not let them say the word "masturbate" in 1998.

Before Katie Holmes was cast in the role that would make her America's sweetheart-next-door, Blair was this close to landing the role.

"Joe was written to be a tomboy and everyone was coming in being very much a tomboy. We were very close to going with Selma Blair, who was amazing," Williamson told THR. "She read it very tough, with a lot of heart."

However, once he saw Holmes on tape, with "those two big eyes," Williamson knew they had their Joey.

Williamson liked Joshua Jackson so much, he didn't care what role the Mighty Ducks alum played.

"I fell in love with Josh Jackson because he could read any role, Dawson or Pacey," he told THR. "But something wasn't complete and that's when the network said they didn't see Josh as Dawson, and rightfully so. So, I went, 'OK, he's Pacey,' because I knew I wanted him in the show no matter what."

Charlie Hunnam Auditioned, Won Role of Husband

An 18-year-old Charlie Hunnam read for the WB drama in 1999 and, while he didn't land the part, he did meet Katherine Towne at his audition.

They tied the knot in Las Vegas three weeks later and divorced in 2002, "three terrible, painful, expensive years later," as Hunnam put it to the Associated Press in 2017.

Dawson's Creek became so popular that American Eagle inked a deal in 2000 to outfit the actors.

The characters wore mostly AE clothes throughout season three, and the cast appeared in ad campaigns and promos for the clothing line, helping drive the company's net income above $105 million in 2001.

When James Van Der Beek was first cast, the studio wanted him to change his hair.

"We found an ad for The Devil's Own, the movie with Brad Pitt," he recalled to The Daily Beast in 2012. "They said: 'What about Brad Pitt's haircut?' That's how I got my season one haircut."

Holmes dated Jackson early in the show's run, before Pacey and Joey realized they opposite-of-hated each other.

"I'm just going to say that I met somebody last year," Holmes told Rolling Stone in 1998, not denying that the somebody was Jackson. "I fell in love, I had my first love, and it was something so incredible and indescribable that I will treasure it always. And that I feel so fortunate because he's now one of my best friends. It's weird, it's almost like a Dawson-and-Joey type thing now."

Plus one more nugget: "He's been in the business so long," she added, "and he's really helped me. I respect him as a friend and a professional."

When Kerr Smith first signed on to join the show as Joey's new boyfriend, he had no idea the character would eventually come out and be part of the first-ever gay kiss on TV.

"I always knew I wanted Jack to come out of the closet, but I didn't even tell [Smith]," Williamson said at the ATX TV Festival. "Let the audience love him, then let's have him come out of the closet and have Joey have to deal with that—and then that would eventually drive her back to [Dawson]."

More poignantly, Williamson has said that every character on the show inherited traits from him, including Jack.

“Every single character has a trait of me in them,” he told Entertainment Weekly in 2018. “I had just, in my 20s, gone through the coming-out process and had told my parents I was gay. I had taken that whole journey, and I wanted a character on the show to represent that journey and to represent that side of me."

Jack's coming out episode, cowritten by Williamson and producer Greg Berlanti, was inspired by true events.

"A friend of mine had a story that I brought in that he got outed accidentally," Berlanti told EW, "because he wrote a love poem that it was so clear to everyone else that it was about a guy.”

Michelle Williams and Busy Philipps' best-friendship, which first blossomed on Dawson's Creek, is still going strong to this day.

“I’m so in love with her,” Williams told People of her bestie at a 2016 screening of Manchester by the Sea, one of many red carpet date nights for the besties. “She’s proof that the love of your life does not have to be a man! That’s the love of my life right there.”

Philipps is also godmother to Williams' daughter Matilda Ledger, who was born in 2005.

Dawson finally losing his virginity was such a big show moment that Van Der Beek brought a very special gift to set the day the scene was filmed.

"I remember bringing champagne for the crew—Dawson finally lost his virginity!" he told The Daily Beast.

Before starring on One Tree Hill, Chad Michael Murray had an arc on Dawson's Creek playing Charlie, a love interest for Jen and Joey.

But while Charlie got around, Murray didn't seem to make a lot of friends during his first stint in North Carolinav (OTH later filmed there).

During a Paley panel in 2009, Philipps called him "a douche," later saying, "Don't worry. I'm not real worried about burning bridges with CMM."

Van Der Beek added, "He's actually come a long way." Post-event, Philipps tweeted, "Just finished the dawson's creek panel. Maybe I was too harsh on chadM2… Nah."

Murray, meanwhile, hasn't stirred the pot, saying in 2015 that he learned a lot from the experience.

“I had the opportunity to learn from people who had been doing it for a couple of years longer than I was when I walked into the Dawson’s cast,” he told Cosmpolitan.com in 2015. “You know, Michelle and James and Katie and Josh—they really kind of guided me, because they’d already been around for five, six years, maybe longer. And if they had the time, they were showing me the ropes. I had no idea what lighting was, I had no idea about a lot of the technical aspects of what we do, and so I’m grateful for that experience.”

Just a sampling of the famous faces, ranging from the already familiar to future huge stars, who appeared on Dawson's Creek over the years: Seth Rogen, Jane Lynch, Julie Bowen, Scott Foley, Jensen Ackles, Hilarie Burton, Rachel Leigh Cook, Ali Larter and Oliver Hudson.

Young Americans was a short-lived spinoff centering on Pacey's friend Will Krudski (Rodney Scott) and his boarding school classmates at Rawley Academy.

Also starring Ian Somerhalder and Kate Bosworth, it was canceled after just one season.

The Show Almost Ended With Joey Picking Dawson

The show's main love triangle officially disassembled when Joey chose Pacey in the 2003 series finale.

But it almost didn't turn out that way, as Williamson first envisioned Dawson getting the girl. But halfway through writing the finale, Williamson realized that a happy ending for that couple wasn't "what the show was set to be."

"I wanted it to be a twist on the teen genre but also wanted it to be surprising, honest and real and say something about soul mates and what soul mates can be," he explained at the ATX TV Festival. "That's why we did it that way. When you left the show in that last moment, they're a family and everyone got what they wanted. There was fulfillment and they were all happy."

At the last minute, he changed his mind and the rest is TV history. But Williamson admitted his mom, who played for Team Dawson, was not happy.

In the finale, which jumped ahead five years, the group had to deal with the devastating loss of Jen.

"Dealing with the death of one of their own was the final thing that thrust them into adulthood forever. Dawson's Creek was a coming-of-age story and that was the idea behind that ending," Williamson explained of the decision. "That's why we killed Jen, because I wanted them to deal with a death of one their own as that final lesson."

Some of the executive producers who get their start on Dawson's?

Julie Plec (who went on to gift us with The Vampire Diaries and The Originals), Berlanti (Everwood, Arrow, The Flash, Riverdale...the list goes on and on, and that doesn't even include his movies), Rob Thomas (Veronica Mars and iZombie), Jenny Bicks (Sex and the City), Anna Fricke (Being Human), Dana Baratta (Jessica Jones) and many more.

#867. David Walliams Denies Sexual Misconduct Allegations

British comedian David Walliams responded to allegations of sexual misconduct published by The Guardian and ITV, denying claims against him: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law."

After The Guardian and ITV published a wide-ranging exposé accusing the former Britain's Got Talent judge of sexual misconduct, including sexual harassment, grooming and abusing his power to sexually prey on women and teenagers as young as 15, he broke his silence to vehemently deny the allegations.

"Looking back, I realize that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with," Walliams, 55, said in a Nov. 10 statement to the outlets, which joined forces for a three-year joint investigation into the accusations made against him. "I realize I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret."

"Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did," the comedian continued. "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me." (The age of consent in the U.K. is 16.)

The article was published earlier on Nov. 10, days after a judge rejected Walliams's injunction to prevent its publication. (Walliams, whose attorney said in court he had attempted suicide twice in the months leading up to the publication, per The Guardian, was seeking psychiatric treatment.) Multiple women—who were identified with pseudonyms after agreeing to speak with the publications under the condition of anonymity—accused Walliams of being "predatory" and "pushy" during the alleged interactions beginning in 2003.

Two of his accusers alleged that they met the children's book author when they were minors, including a woman identified as Alex, who said she was 15 when she met him at an autograph signing in 2004 where she gave him her cover letter in hopes of exploring a comedy writing career, according to The Guardian.

Alex alleged that she and Walliams exchanged multiple emails—which were included in the publication—and occasionally spoke on the phone for two years. She said that he suggested that he could help her succeed in the comedy world.

By 17, she said that they were having sex. "I think I was groomed, 100 percent," she told The Guardian. "We met when I was 15 and he was promising to help me and was a figure of authority and someone that I looked to for guidance and help."

Another woman, referred to as Jade, also alleged she was 15 when she had met Walliams. She said that after the then-36-year-old reached out to her on MySpace in 2007—which Jade said clearly showed her date of birth—he invited her to his home, where he kissed her.

Other accounts—ITV and The Guardian cited speaking with 30 sources with first-hand knowledge of his behavior—were from women between 18 and early 20s who alleged Walliams tried to use his fame and wealth to coerce them into sex.

One such accuser, Sarah, 18, alleged that Walliams took an interest in her after meeting him during filming for Britain's Got Talent, according to The Guardian. He eventually invited the starstruck teen to his London home, with her alleging that he attempted to have sex with her while she was drunk and unable to walk properly, but her friend intervened. She said she and her friend ultimately slept in a spare bedroom.

Walliams' attorney emphasized that his client denied any wrongdoing with all of the women, also refuting Sarah's allegation that he got her "drunk to take advantage of her."

E! News has reached out to Walliams' reps and HarperCollins UK for comment and has not yet heard back.

Unspecified allegations were previously made against Walliams—who shares a son with ex Lara Stone—by at least five female employees at his publisher HarperCollins in December 2025, per The Guardian.

The company ultimately dropped him, telling The Telegraph at the time, "After careful consideration, and under the leadership of its new CEO, HarperCollins UK has decided not to publish any new titles by David Walliams."

Walliams's agent told the outlet in a statement that his client "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately."

#866. Who are the main candidates for the Aberdeen job?

Steven Pressley, John McGlynn and Steve Clarke have all been mentioned in despatches

Another season, another managerial sacking at Aberdeen.

Stephen Robinson's departure on Monday made it five dismissals since the spring of 2021.

The Northern Irishman followed Stephen Glass, Jim Goodwin, Barry Robson and Jimmy Thelin in making an abrupt exit on the watch of chairman Dave Cormack.

Most of the quintet have lasted less than a year and, although Thelin ended the Dons' 35-year wait to win the Scottish Cup, the general trend has been one of perceived underachievement in Scottish Premiership.

Derek McInnes, now with Rangers after spells at Kilmarnock and Heart of Midlothian, was the last Pittodrie boss to regularly deliver consistent results in the top flight and consequent European qualification.

So who could be next? And what qualities does such a manager require?

'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign'

Aberdeen sack Robinson after league slump

Falkirk add goals and grit to McGlynn's guile on rapid rise

Two names mentioned fairly early on after Robinson's exit were Dundee's Steven Pressley and Falkirk's John McGlynn.

Both have impressed in the Premiership this past 17 months, drawing admirers for style of play and good results.

Falkirk are third in the division, two places above Dundee, and McGlynn's side were sixth last season, again two places higher than Pressley's men.

Former Aberdeen defender Richard Foster said the pair are "the two that stand out for me domestically" and said of Elgin-born Pressley on BBC Radio Scotland's Breakfast: "I know he's got a quiet, laid-back demeanour, but I think in the dressing room, he commands respect.

"The players at Dundee seem to love playing for him.

"He knows the game very well. Having played at Hearts, having played at Celtic, he knows what it's like to be at a huge club."

Former Hearts, Hibernian and Scotland midfielder Michael Stewart has been impressed with McGlynn's track record of signing players.

Speaking on McGlynn on BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound, Stewart said: "John McGlynn puts the miles in.

"He's up and down the road down south. He's up and around all over Scotland. He knows what the players are that are perhaps not in the eye of many others. He knows them intimately before they arrive at Falkirk.

"So it's no great surprise that his success rate with recruitment is pretty, pretty good.

"I would not be surprised if, whenever one or two of the bigger jobs start coming up... rather than being sort of an outsider, I think he'll be right in the hunt for some of those jobs."

Former Celtic and Hibs midfielder Scott Allan says McGlynn is "very tactically astute" and commented: "I love everything that John McGlynn does. Everybody in Scottish football can respect the job he's done there, the consistency.

"He's one of the most prepared managers, if not the most prepared manager for any sort of set-up that he faces week-to-week and he's shown that.

"It's a fantastic job he's done over the last three or four years. He deserves all the credit that comes his way."

It may seem like a lifetime ago, but it's actually only been five months since Steve Clarke stepped down as Scotland head coach.

The 63-year-old, like McGlynn, has vast coaching experience, including in Scotland after a two-year spell with Kilmarnock.

Clarke oversaw three qualifications to major tournaments with Scotland, ending long waits to appear at the European Championship and World Cup.

As well as managerial stints at West Bromwich Albion and Reading, Clarke has worked at Chelsea, Liverpool and Newcastle United, so little would daunt the former right-back.

Appointing Clarke would be a statement by Aberdeen and the challenge of restoring the club to competitiveness may be a compelling one for the man himself.

However, along with McGlynn, geography may play a part and their candidacy could depend on whether personal circumstances allow a switch to the north east.

Wigan Athletic boss and former Scotland centre-half Gary Caldwell has also been linked with the Pittodrie job. The 44-year-old cut his managerial teeth with the Latics and returned there earlier this year after spells in charge of Chesterfield, Partick Thistle and Exeter City.

Swede Thelin stands out as one of the few overseas managers Aberdeen have had.

Yes, Goodwin and Robinson hail from Ireland and Northern Ireland respectively, but both are very much embedded in Scottish football after spending so much time at various clubs north of the border.

The only other non-Scottish manager to grace the Pittodrie home dugout was the Dane, Ebbe Skovdahl, from 1999-2002.

As such, it is fair to say Aberdeen have not experimented too much with foreign coaches and have tended to go with faces familiar to the Scottish top flight.

With a German, Lutz Pfannenstiel, as the sporting director, Aberdeen look further afield this time?

It has become the vogue in the Premiership of late, with Hearts, Hibs and Motherwell going foreign, with Belgian Wouter Vrancken, Dutchman Marink Reedijk and Swede Alfred Johansson in recent months.

Should Pfannenstiel unearth the next Jens Berthel Askou, formerly of Motherwell, Dons fans will be delighted.

Podcast: What is going wrong at Aberdeen?

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/p0pm7gkd

Former Aberdeen defender Stuart Duff is in interim charge of Aberdeen following the departures of Robinson, assistant Brian Kerr and coach Stephen Craigan.

The Dons are second bottom of the Premiership, two points above Kilmarnock.

Unless an appointment is made during the international break, Duff faces taking Aberdeen to face Kilmarnock on 21 November before visiting Rangers three days later, with their next home game being against Dundee on 28 November.

Confidence is low after seven league defeats so far this season, but the tightly-packed middle section of the league means Aberdeen are only a couple of wins off the top six.

#865. Pochettino’s Manchester United interest is as natural as it is disruptive to the US

The former Tottenham manager is always going to be a subject of interest, but United’s job carries a rare power

As Mauricio Pochettino left the podium to close his final press conference of the last international window, he offered an ambiguous farewell.

“See you next …” Pochettino began as he headed to the tunnels of Allianz Field in Saint Paul, before cutting his sentence short. Then, a bit of a sing-song: “See you next, see you next.”

You don’t need an AI clanker’s autocomplete function to try closing the sentence. “See you next month” would have been synonymous with “see you next window”, after all. Still, the farewell felt poignant given questions about whether Pochettino was going to last a full four-year cycle as US men’s national team head coach.

In hindsight, maybe he had omitted adding something along the lines of: see you next, before I’m off to my next project.

From the moment that Pochettino and US Soccer announced his contract renewal in August, it was tough for many to imagine he would don his lavish safari shirts on the US sideline at the 2030 World Cup. This was Mauricio Pochettino, after all, a name brand in club management whose résumé teemed with unfinished business. Few great coaches hang their hat on being Premier League and Champions League runners-up.

Gone are the days where clubs with major financial considerations pull the plug on a whim. The time to strike is now at the start of an international window, when the next game isn’t for another couple of weeks. This serves as a crucial time to meet the squad, put them through their paces and hatch an initial scheme to stop the rot.

That puts international federations like US Soccer in an unenviable position. Pochettino is among the most eligible options for the Big Clubs, ensuring his continuing presence on managerial wishlists. And as long as that remains the case, the most likely window for advances from club suitors will be right in the stretch of time where a national team coach works hardest.

In September, that meant reheating years-old discourses about the apparent irresistibility of Tottenham Hotspur. Before the World Cup, Milan had come calling. And now, the focus turns to Old Trafford.

The attraction is logical. For over a decade, United have tested every managerial archetype possible since Sir Alex Ferguson called time on his illustrious career. Domestic options who punched above their weight class; chronic winners; onetime supernovas, with implosion all but inevitable; club legends; club custodians; young options ready for a Premier League closeup. Their tenures all ended the same.

Pochettino blends some of the best traits of Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho with a record of doing the work United hoped would happen under Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. His work building Tottenham into a threat on all fronts bolstered his culture-building cachet, showing his success at Espanyol and Southampton could scale. Even though his time at Paris Saint-Germain failed to yield their long-coveted Champions League title, he had experienced managing the egos of Neymar, Mbappé and Messi. Chelsea tested his tolerance for ownership-meddling. All of these factors inform Manchester United at present.

So no, the idea of Pochettino leaving the US so soon into his second term is hardly a shock. If it wasn’t to be United, or Tottenham, then he’d be a hot commodity if Real Madrid were to quickly abandon their reunion with Mourinho. If not them, then perhaps Milan again if their campaign were to sour before the festive season. And so on.

US Soccer deserves some credit for adequately preparing. For one thing, Pochettino’s retention was only made possible thanks to a billionaire super-donor, Ken Griffin. So while his wages dwarfed those of his predecessors, it hadn’t directly come at the expense of the federation’s other teams, initiatives or grassroots efforts.

The real boon is his release clause, a reported $10m (£7.5m) option that only a Big Club could afford to spring. Had Pochettino left after the World Cup, coach and federation would have parted with nothing more exchanged than a handshake and some pleasantries. Instead, they forged an insurance policy to make up for what could have been if Pochettino had stayed for a full cycle.

Of course, piles of money don’t qualify for World Cups. Should this international window be Pochettino’s last with the US, the onus will be on the federation to do what it couldn’t this summer and find an alternative to lead a program into an exciting new era. It would be a boon to the federation if that $10m pot was kept on standby to help foot the next coach’s wages, keeping the pool of possible candidates open and deep.

US Soccer will need to nail the next hire to reassure fans who fell for the team during their entertaining run at this year’s World Cup. That will probably be a project-by-committee, as the federation hasn’t seemed antsy to replace Matt Crocker after he quit his role as sporting director in April. And, if Pochettino was unlikely to be in the role all the way until 2030, perhaps it is a blessing that a split comes while the cycle is still dawning.

#864. Kompany back at Bayern training after collapse

Head coach Vincent Kompany has returned to Bayern Munich's training ground after collapsing at the end of last month.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train.

Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Bayern said in a statement: "Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground since the start of the week."

However, the Bundesliga leaders did not hold a training session, with most players away on international duty.

English coach Aaron Danks has been in charge during Kompany's absence, leading Bayern to four victories and a draw.

They face Cologne next on 20 November after the end of the two-week international break.
